extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in folklore, popular science, and lunar beliefs
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and discusses traditional customs, ritual prescriptions, and popular/scientific criteria regarding the moon (superstitions, divination practices, etiquette for sighting, and arguments about lunar habitability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Astrological scheduling of personal and agricultural acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals time bodily and practical acts according to planetary and lunar positions: e.g., 'He will not open a vein till he has asked leave of the planets. He will not commit his seed to the earth when the soil, but when the moon, requires it. He will have his hair cut when the moon is either in Leo, that his locks may stare like the lion's shag, or in Aries, that they may curl like a ram's horn.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given include avoiding bleeding without planetary permission; planting and sexual agriculture timed to lunar phases; cutting hair in Leo or Aries for desired hair texture; planting in Taurus because it is a 'fixed' sign to make trees take root; avoiding the sea when Mars is prominent to avert pirates. These are prescriptive folk rules assigning optimum or unlucky timings to actions based on signs/planets.

rubrics_metrics.name: New moon auspicious for commencements
rubrics_metrics.description: The new moon is considered pre-eminently auspicious for commencements — 'for all kinds of building up, and beginning de novo.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescribed actions at the new moon: erect or move into houses; conclude marriages; count money (believed to be increased then); cut hair and nails; gather healing herbs and pure dew. The text explicitly states 'Money counted at that period will be increased.' This is a prescriptive timing rule for beginnings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full and waning moon appropriate for breaking down, cleaning, and ending tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: The full moon (and especially the waning moon) is the time for pulling down and thinking of the end of all things; practical tasks of reduction and cleaning are scheduled to the waning moon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: cut timber, mow grass, make hay while the moon wanes; stuff feather-beds and kill newly plucked feathers during the waning moon so they are 'killed completely'; wash linen by the waning moon 'that the dirt may disappear with the dwindling light.' The full moon is associated with endings rather than beginnings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid assuming new clothes during the moon's decline
rubrics_metrics.description: It was deemed unlucky to assume a new dress when the moon was in her decline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted reasoning: the garment will 'continue long' not because of its quality but because the wearer lacks leisure or liberty to wear it — a folk rationalization. This is an anti-pattern: beginning the wearing of new clothes during waning moon is considered inauspicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blessing the new moon ritual (Kitzur Sh'lu procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed procedural prescription for 'Blessing the new moon': perform outdoors, wear best dress (especially at Sabbath close), wait 3–7 days after birth according to authority, give one glance at the moon then do not look again, and recite the 'Form of Prayer for the New Moon' with specified actions and repetitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stepwise rules given: 'When about to sanctify the new moon, one should straighten his feet (as at the Shemonah-esreh) and give one glance at the moon before he begins to repeat the ritual blessing, and having commenced it he should not look at her at all.' Then begin 'In the united name of the Holy and Blessed One...' and proceed word for word without haste but with solemn deliberation. Specific performance elements: meditate on initials forming 'Jacob' and repeat three times; skip three times while repeating a sentence thrice; repeat three times forwards and backwards a sentence; say to neighbour three times 'Peace be unto you' and receive threefold response; say 'David, the King of Israel, liveth and existeth!' three times; conclude with 'May a good omen and good luck be upon us and upon all Israel! Amen!' This is a prescriptive ritual rubric with explicit order and repetition counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divination of military expediency by lunar timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Some communities consult lots/divination and decline to engage in battle before the new moon — e.g., among the Germans Ariovistus delayed engagement because matrons divined that 'it was not the will of heaven that the Germans should conquer, if they engaged in battle before the new moon.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Folk rule: defer military action until auspicious lunar timing determined by divination; treating negative divinatory results as reason to postpone engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harvest-moon pillow divination (items and cards under pillow)
rubrics_metrics.description: A harvest-moon divination practice: place under the pillow a prayer-book open at the matrimonial service, plus specific items (key, ring, flower, willow sprig, small heart-cake, crust of bread) and a set of playing cards (ten of clubs, nine of hearts, ace of spades, ace of diamonds), wrapped and laid under the pillow with hands crossed while reciting a short invocation to the moon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dream-symbol interpretations are given: storms = trouble; ring or ace of diamonds = marriage; bread = industrious life; cake = prosperous life; flowers = joy; willow = treachery in love; spades = death; diamonds = money; clubs = a foreign land; hearts = illegitimate children; keys = rise to trust and power; birds = many children; geese = marry more than once. This is an explicit protocol for producing and reading divinatory dreams.

rubrics_metrics.name: New-moon dream-divination for revealing future spouse (regional variants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple regional customs where maidens go out at the first new moon and perform spoken formulas or actions (curtseying, sitting astride gates, standing at stiles, invoking the moon) in order to see their future husbands in dreams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variants cited: in Berkshire recite 'New moon... Grant this night that I may see He who my true love is to be.' In Devonshire turn one's back to the moon at a stile and recite a longer rhyme describing the future husband. In Scotland women make a curtsey to the new moon and recite a formula 'All haille to thee, moon...' In Ireland point with a knife, invoke the Holy Trinity, place the knife under the pillow and keep silence. The guidance emphasizes locality-specific wording and small ritual actions (curtsey, turn back, place knife/ring/cake under pillow) as essential to producing the dream omen.

rubrics_metrics.name: First new moon ingestion ritual for fortunes (white ingredients and verses)
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipe-based divination for the first new moon of the year: take a pint of clear spring water, infuse the white of an egg laid by a white hen, a glass of white wine, three peeled white almonds, and a tablespoonful of white rose-water; drink in three draughts on going to bed while repeating specified verses three times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given poem to be recited three times; dream-interpretation mapping: dreaming of pure water = sign of poverty; tasting beer = middling cheer; tasting wine = wealth and pleasure; 'the stronger the drink, the better the cheer.' The protocol specifies ingredient colors, drink count, volume, and formula recitation counts, making it a strict prescriptive ritual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Day-of-week effect on lunar luck
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief that the day of the week on which a new or full moon falls affects luck: certain days are considered inauspicious for lunar change depending on region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in north Italy Wednesday is dreaded for a lunar change; in south of France Friday is inauspicious; many rural English districts dislike Friday's new moon. Rural rhymes: 'Friday's moon, Come when it wool, It comes too soon.' 'Saturday's new and Sunday's full, Never was good, and never wull.' 'A Saturday moon, If it comes once in seven years, Comes once too soon.' The guidance is to consider day-of-week overlays when interpreting lunar omens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constraints on the medium of first sighting of the new moon
rubrics_metrics.description: Folk rules prescribe what you may look through when first sighting the new moon: the medium (veil, window-pane, trees, glass, handkerchief) is believed to affect the omen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific rules: in Staffordshire it's unlucky to see the new moon through trees; some fear seeing it through a veil; look through an unwashed silk handkerchief to multiply the moons you see (as many threads equals years until marriage); it is widely believed unlucky to see the new moon through glass (window-pane) — may lead to broken glass before the moon is out — and one should rather go into open air. These are prescriptive restrictions about how to make the first sighting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have silver in pocket when first seeing the new moon
rubrics_metrics.description: Common belief that it is unlucky to see the new moon for the first time without silver (coins of silver) in one's pocket; other metals are considered ineffective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted belief: 'The ill-luck of having no silver money -- coins of other metals being of no avail -- when you first see or hail a new moon, is still a common belief from Cornwall to Caithness, as well as in Ireland.' Explanatory note connects silver's whiteness and lunar symbolism as justification. Practical ritual guidance: carry silver and turn it over when sighting to ward off misfortune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moon position relative to observer predicts fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: The direction/position of the new moon when first seen (right/left/straight before you) is taken as a prognostication: right or before = good fortune; left or behind = bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defoe-quoted rule: 'To see a new moon the first time after her change, on the right hand, or directly before you, betokens the utmost good fortune that month; as to have her on your left, or behind you... foreshows the worst.' Practical implication: where you first see the moon (relative to your body) is treated as a divinatory sign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid major undertakings or movements during the moon's wane
rubrics_metrics.description: Waning moon is generally considered an unlucky time to begin important business, move house, or slaughter animals: many regions avoid engaging in important undertakings during the moon's wane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in Orkney it is reckoned unlucky to move during the waning of the moon; in Kirkmichael and the Highlands nothing important is begun during the moon's wane; killing an animal in the moon's decrease makes the flesh 'unwholesome,' and accounts of bacon shrinking in boiling are attributed to butchering during the wane. Conversely, increase and full are emblems of rising and flourishing fortune, and are preferred for beginnings such as marriage or provisioning stores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moon phases as emblems of fortune cycles
rubrics_metrics.description: The moon's increase, full growth, and wane are used metaphorically and practically as emblems of rising, established, and declining fortune, and communities regulate activities accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual commentary: 'The moon in her increase, full growth, and in her wane, are with them the emblems of a rising, flourishing, and declining fortune.' The guidance is both symbolic and prescriptive: choose phases to align undertakings with anticipated fortune (waxing/ full = favourable; waning = avoid).

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief in lunar influence on disease, death, and bodily functions (periodicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular theories link the moon (and tides) to periodicity in disease and the timing of death: e.g., some traditions assert people die at ebb not flow; periodic fevers or 'lucid intervals' in mental disease are connected with lunar cycles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities cited (Dr. Winslow, others) consider periodicity an important symptom in disease and discuss alleged correlations between tide phases and death timing. The text treats the claim as contested and recommends specialist medical investigation; nonetheless this belief functions as a folk criterion for timing or interpreting medical events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three methodological avenues to assess lunar inhabitation: observation, induction, analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Framing of the scientific question 'Is the moon inhabited?' into three investigative approaches: observation (empirical telescope/photography), induction (reasoning from necessary conditions), and analogy (inference from known cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance explains strengths/limitations of each: observation limited by distance and current instrument power; induction depends on identifying necessary conditions for life (atmosphere, water, seasons, day/night cycle); analogy can suggest possibilities but only shadow the substance. The text recommends combining methods and notes photographic lunar mapping as a promising observational aid (Lockyer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for lunar habitability (necessary physical conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: To render the moon habitable by beings akin to Earth life, there must be atmosphere, water, changing seasons, and alternations of day and night. The lunar day length (very long exposure and darkness) is also a factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes that extreme temperature swings from a very long lunar day (each portion exposed to the sun for nearly 14 of our days — the passage gives a figure 'as long as 291 of ours' in one spot) make habitation by Earth-like organisms implausible without substantial atmosphere/water. This is an inductive standard: presence/absence of atmosphere and water are decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive evidence against substantial lunar atmosphere/water (authoritative judgments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements by scientific authorities concluding that if the moon has an atmosphere it is extremely rarefied and that lunar 'seas' are probably not bodies of water in any significant quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations and paraphrases: La Place: 'The lunar atmosphere, if any such exists, is of an extreme rarity... no terrestrial animal could live or respire at the surface of the moon.' Russell Hind: lunar 'seas' if water exist at all must be in very small quantity. Humboldt, Grant, Lardner express scepticism about any substantial gaseous envelope or vapour atmosphere. Use of these authorities functions as an inductive rubric: modest/absent atmosphere and negligible water argue strongly against Earth-like habitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational methods for lunar mapping and inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation of observational tools and techniques for studying the moon: telescopes of very high magnification and lunar photography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noted practical points: the 'Moon Committee' recommended a power of 1,000 though instruments/nights that bear it are few; increased magnification reduces effective distance; Norman Lockyer: photography allows fixing many points on the lunar surface and aids accurate mapping. This is procedural guidance on how to pursue the observational avenue.
